To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the antiviral effect of 90K on nascent HIV- 1 virions is conserved within primates, with the exception of rhesus monkeys, and that the absence of the antiviral property in rhesus monkey 90K is caused by a single amino acid substitution in the BTB domain.
the cellular 90K glycoprotein is a potent inhibitor of HIV-1 infectivity, but that this function is lost in the 90K protein from rhesus monkeys.

the antiviral effect of the cellular 90K factor is conserved within the primate species but not within the rhesus monkey species, and that a single amino acid change in a specific region of the protein is sufficient to rescue the antivirally impaired 90K from the rhesus species.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the conservation of the antiviral properties of a cellular protein in primate species.
the identification of a novel antiviral protein and with its conservation across primate species.
understanding how a cellular protein can modulate the infectivity of a virus.
